scenario_constructions: Esperanza Haldane and the pantry are fictional (corpus convention). The BLS prices are real. The funding rule that excludes dry beans, the $12,000 monthly budget, the one-protein-per-order contract and the stand-in of BLS national averages for supplier quotes are stated scenario constructions (MA1, MA2, Background). The decision date (a Friday in mid-September 2024) is chosen so that August 2024 is the latest BLS month already published.
sensitivity_note: SPEC 6: this case touches food insecurity and family hardship. Some students and their families may use pantries. Frame the Hero as a professional making a budget decision, do not ask students to imagine specific families going without, and discuss the beans exclusion as a funding rule, not a judgment on what families should eat. Full note in FACILITATOR.md.

deliverables.text: A table of grams of protein per dollar for Eggs and for Chicken at the August 2024 prices, with the dozen-to-grams and pound-to-grams conversions shown as equivalent ratios.
Grams of protein bought in one month and in the quarter under each option at August 2024 prices, and the difference in grams.
The margin (gap divided by the winner's value, as a percent) and the break-even price for each option as a percent change from its August 2024 price.
Two blended orders (50/50 and one the student chooses): grams per dollar against the two pure options, and one sentence on what a blend can and cannot do.
A line chart of monthly grams of protein per dollar for both options, January 2006 through August 2024, with the August 2024 point marked.
Dry-bean grams per dollar at August 2024 prices, the difference from the chosen option and how many times as many; a paragraph on what the metric leaves out and what the funding rule costs.

appendices.title: The Order and the Latest Prices
Monthly Price History, January 2006 through August 2024

balance.argument_a: Eggs: in the Background-visible record (224 months, Jan 2006-Aug 2024) eggs deliver more protein per dollar than chicken in 209 months, with a median of 42.1 against 30.7 grams per dollar; as late as June 2024 eggs were ahead by 9.1% (27.76 against 25.22). The two earlier stretches in which chicken led lasted 7 and 6 months and then reversed, and August 2024 is only the second month of the current one. Because the order is price-floating, an egg price 8.9% below $3.204 (that is $2.918) erases chicken's lead, and eggs are easy for families to cook and accept.
balance.argument_b: Chicken: at the prices the board will actually pay when it plans, chicken delivers 25.82 grams per dollar against 23.52, a lead of 8.9% (gap divided by the winner) or 82,955 grams over the quarter. Chicken's price has been stable ($3.946 to $4.229 over Jun 2023-Aug 2024) while egg prices have swung, so chicken carries less price risk; eggs need a fall of 8.9% in price to match, while a plan on history asks the board to bet on a reversal that has not yet happened.
balance.margin_basis: Margin = (winner - loser) / winner on grams of protein per dollar at the August 2024 BLS prices: (25.82 - 23.52) / 25.82 = 8.9%. The retired gap/loser figure is 9.8%, which equals chicken's break-even rise in price; the convention is stated once and used everywhere.
balance.convention: gap divided by the winner's value

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The quarter's egg price relative to the August 2024 planning price is a forecast: no amount of research tells Esperanza next quarter's price. The case states the floating order (MA2) and asks students to defend a bet on it.
The quarter's chicken price relative to the August 2024 planning price is a forecast of a future price and cannot be known in advance.

The 50 g edible weight of a large egg is a published USDA value that exists but could not be re-fetched from the authoring sandbox (FoodData Central unreachable 2026-10-28); a good-faith value from an earlier read is used. A 50 percent swing is outside any plausible range (+/-5 percent leaves the winner unchanged). Exception, not template: re-confirm at publish.

The 12.56 g per 100 g protein value is a published USDA value that could not be re-fetched from the authoring sandbox; a 50 percent swing is physically implausible (+/-5 percent leaves the winner unchanged). Exception, not template: re-confirm at publish.

The 22.5 g per 100 g raw chicken breast protein value is a published USDA value that could not be re-fetched from the authoring sandbox; a 50 percent swing is physically implausible (+/-5 percent leaves the winner unchanged; 23.1 gives 11.3 percent). Exception, not template: re-confirm at publish.

context_glossary.desc: A place that gives groceries to people who need them, usually free. Many pantries get most of their food from a larger food bank.
A large warehouse-style nonprofit that collects and stores donated and purchased food and passes it to smaller pantries and meal programs.
The chain of refrigerators, freezers and refrigerated trucks that keeps food at a safe temperature from the supplier all the way to the shelf.

context_why_notes.D1: Why grams per dollar: eggs are sold by the dozen and chicken by the pound, so neither price can be compared until both are turned into the same unit of protein for a dollar.
context_why_notes.D2: Why scale to the budget: a rate is only useful once it is multiplied by what you can actually spend.
context_why_notes.D3: Why a percent of the winner and break-even prices: the margin says how close the call is; the break-even says how much a price has to move before the call flips.
context_why_notes.D4: Why test a blend: it shows whether a split order could ever beat the better single option.
context_why_notes.D5: Why a chart of the whole record: one month is a snapshot; the line shows how long each option has led before.
context_why_notes.D6: Why price the rule: a rule that limits choices has a cost, and naming it lets the board decide whether the rule is worth keeping.

context_note: Added 3 story terms (food pantry, food bank, cold-chain); all appear in case.md. 'walk-in cooler', 'Grade A' and 'cash-and-carry' style terms skipped: context explains them. No tooltip states a result. No visual added: the case is a table-and-chart decision and Deliverable D5 asks the student to draw the chart; an illustrative chart would pre-empt it.

math_glossary.desc: A comparison of two quantities by division, such as grams of protein to dollars.
A ratio that compares two quantities with different units, such as dollars per pound.
A rate written for exactly one of something, such as grams of protein for one dollar.
An equation that says two ratios are equal; scaling a rate to a budget uses one.
How much a quantity went up or down, as a percent of where it started.
A single number that stands for a whole set of values; BLS average prices are one.
An average in which some values count more than others; a blended order is one.
A chart that joins points over time with a line so a trend can be seen.

research_notes.decision_date_fix: The concept sheet placed the order in August 2024 while using the August 2024 BLS average; that month is not yet published in August. The order is placed in mid-September 2024 for an October-December quarter, so August 2024 is the latest published month. Post-decision twist data therefore covers Oct-Dec 2024 (and Jan-Mar 2025 as the next-quarter extension), not Sep-Nov.
